'''umbrate†''' (um′brāt), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''umbratus'', pp. of ''umbrare'' (> F. ''ombrer''), shade, overshadow, < ''umbra'', shade, shadow: see ''umber''<sup>1</sup>.] To shade; shadow; foreshadow.

'''umbrated''' (um′brā-ted), ''a.'' [< ''umbrate'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] In ''her.'': (''a'') Shadowed, or casting a shadow. (''b'') Same as ''entrailed.'' Neither of these uses is strictly heraldic.
{{smaller block|Those ensignes which are borne ''umbrated.''
{{right|''Bossewell'', Workes of Armorie (1572), p. 25. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''umbratic†''' (um-brat′ik), ''a.'' [< L. ''umbraticus'', of or pertaining to shade or shadow, being in retirement, secluded, < ''umbra'', shade: see ''umbra'', ''umber''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''umbrage.''] '''1.''' Shadowy; foreshadowing; hence, casting shadows.
{{smaller block|Those ''umbratick'' representations (or insinuations) did obtain their substance, validity, and effect.
{{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, II. xxvii.}}}}
'''2.''' Keeping in the shade or in retirement; secluded; retired.

'''umbratical†''' (um-brat′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' [< ''umbratic'' + ''-al.''] Same as ''umbratic.''
{{smaller block|Whole volumes dispatched by the ''umbratical'' doctors on all sides.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Discoveries.}}}}

'''umbratile†''' (um′bra-til), ''a.'' [< L. ''umbratilis'', remaining in the shade, retired, < ''umbra'', shade: see ''umbra.''] '''1.''' Being in the shade or in retirement; secluded.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|umbrage|6574|umbrella-ant}}</noinclude>shadow: see ''umbra'', ''umber''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Shade; a shadow; obscurity.

{{smaller block|We are past the twilights of conversion, and the ''umbrages'' of the world, and walk in the light of God.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 841.}}}}

{{smaller block|His [Wordsworth’s] angels and fiends are human thoughts and feelings, and he can awake them at will from the ''umbrage'' of the old Rydal woods.
{{right|''Noctes Ambrosianæ'', April, 1832.}}}}

'''2.''' That which affords a shade; specifically, a screen of trees or foliage.

<poem>The linnets warble, captive none, but lur’d
By food to haunt the ''umbrage''; all the glade
Is life, is music, liberty, and love.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''W. Mason'', English Garden, iv.}}}}

<poem>Into trackless forest set
With trees, whose lofty ''umbrage'' met.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', Tour in Scotland (1814), The Brownie’s Cell.}}}}

'''3.''' A slight appearance; an apparition; a shade.

{{smaller block|Some of them being ''umbrages'' . . . rather than realities.
{{right|''Fuller'', Holy War, v. 25. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|A penitent is not taken with ''umbrages'' and appearances, nor quits a real good for an imaginary.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 183.}}}}

{{smaller block|The opinion carries no show of truth nor ''umbrage'' of reason on its side.
{{right|''Woodward.''}}}}

'''4.''' The feeling of being overshadowed, as by another standing in one’s light or way; hence, suspicion of slight or injury; offense; resentment.

{{smaller block|I say, just fear, . . . not out of ''umbrages'', light jealousies, apprehensions afar off, but out of clear foresight of imminent danger.
{{right|''Bacon'', War with Spain.}}}}

{{smaller block|So they parted for that time without the least ''Umbrage'' of Discontent, nor do I hear of any engendered since.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. iii. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Persian ambassador . . . did not care to see any Franks, the port being very suspicious, and the minister very wisely avoided giving ''umbrage'' without any reason.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 100.}}}}
{{smaller block|No part of Henry’s conduct gave such ''umbrage'' to his nobles as the facility with which he resigned himself to the control of favorites. {{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., i. 3.}}}}
='''Syn. 4.''' See ''pique''<sup>2</sup> and ''animosity''.

'''umbrage''' (um′brāj), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''umbraged'', ppr. ''umbraging''. [< ''umbrage'', ''n.''] To shade.
{{smaller block|A ridge or hillock heavily ''umbraged'' with the rounded foliage of evergreen oaks. {{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVI. 733.}}}}

'''umbrageous''' (um-brā′jius), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''umbragious''; < F. ''ombrageux'', shady, < ''ombrage'', shade: see ''umbrage''.] '''1.''' Forming or affording a shade; shading; shady.
{{smaller block|Consider but the rudiment of a tall and ''umbrageous'' tree, from so minute a seed as may be borne away by every blast. {{right|''Evelyn'', True Religion, I. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ash far-stretching his ''umbrageous'' arm.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, i. 311.}}}}
{{smaller block|Do they play as formerly with thy crisp glossy curls, so delicate and ''umbrageous''?
{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Alcibiades and Xenophon.}}}}
'''2.''' Shaded; shady: as, an ''umbrageous'' glen.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Umbrageous'' grots and caves
Of cool recess.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 257.}}}}
'''3†.''' Obscure; doubtful, as if from being darkened or shaded; hence, suspicious; “rather shady.”
{{smaller block|In the present constitution of the Court (which is very ''ombrageous'').{{right|''Sir H. Wotton'', Reliquiæ.}}}}
'''4†.''' Apt or disposed to take offense; taking umbrage.

'''umbrageously''' (um-brā′jius-li), ''adv.'' In an umbrageous manner.

'''umbrageousness''' (um-brā′jius-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being umbrageous; shadiness: as, the ''umbrageousness'' of a tree.

'''umbraid†''' (um-brād′), ''v. t.'' [ME. ''umbrayden'', ''umbreyden''; < ''um-'' + ''braid''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''upbraid''.] To upbraid.
{{smaller block|Whan she of his falsenesse him ''umbreyde''.{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1671.}}
I ''umbrayde'' one, I cast one in the tethe of an offence that he hath done. . . . What though he have done a mysse, it was nat thy parte to ''umbrayde'' hym.{{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 766.}}}}

'''umbraid†''', ''n.'' Strife; contention. ''Halliwell.''

'''umbral''' (um′bral), ''a.'' [< ''umbra'' + ''-al''.] Pertaining to an umbra.—'''Umbral notation''', {{smaller|a notation for determinants invented by the French mathematician Vandermonde (1735–96) in 1772, but substantially known to Leibnitz. Each constituent of the determinant is represented as the product of two letters, one for the row the other for the column, which letters do not, of course, denote quantities, but only the numerical position of the row or columns, so that the product of one of one set by one of the other is equal to a quantity. If the umbral multiplication is commutative, the determinant is symmetrical; if polar, it is skew symmetrical. The name was given by Sylvester.}}

'''Umbral''' (um′bral), ''n.'' [< L. ''umbra'', shade, twilight, + ''-al''.] In the classification of the Paleozoic series of Pennsylvania, according to H. D. Rogers, a group of rocks of great thickness, belonging to the Carboniferous, and lying between the Seral or Millstone-grit and the Vespertine. {{smaller|The Umbral and Vespertine together constitute the Subcarboniferous of some authors, or that part of the Carboniferous which lies below the Millstone-grit.}}

'''umbrate†''' (um′brāt), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''umbratus'', pp. of ''umbrare'' (> F. ''ombrer''), shade, overshadow, < ''umbra'', shade, shadow: see ''umber''<sup>1</sup>.] To shade; shadow; foreshadow.

'''umbrated''' (um′brā-ted), ''a.'' [< ''umbrate'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] In ''her.'': (''a'') Shadowed, or casting a shadow. (''b'') Same as ''entrailed.'' Neither of these uses is strictly heraldic.
{{smaller block|Those ensignes which are borne ''umbrated.''
{{right|''Bossewell'', Workes of Armorie (1572), p. 25. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''umbratic†''' (um-brat′ik), ''a.'' [< L. ''umbraticus'', of or pertaining to shade or shadow, being in retirement, secluded, < ''umbra'', shade: see ''umbra'', ''umber''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''umbrage.''] '''1.''' Shadowy; foreshadowing; hence, casting shadows.
{{smaller block|Those ''umbratick'' representations (or insinuations) did obtain their substance, validity, and effect.
{{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, II. xxvii.}}}}
'''2.''' Keeping in the shade or in retirement; secluded; retired.

'''umbratical†''' (um-brat′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' [< ''umbratic'' + ''-al.''] Same as ''umbratic.''
{{smaller block|Whole volumes dispatched by the ''umbratical'' doctors on all sides.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Discoveries.}}}}

'''umbratile†''' (um′bra-til), ''a.'' [< L. ''umbratilis'', remaining in the shade, retired, < ''umbra'', shade: see ''umbra.''] '''1.''' Being in the shade or in retirement; secluded. {{smaller block|Health that hath not been softened by an ''umbratile'' life still under the roof.{{right|''Bacon.''}}}}
{{smaller block|We must not . . . play the geometrician with our soul, as we may with lines and figures, and things obnoxious to our senses, in this ''umbratile'' state and dependence.
{{right|''Evelyn'', True Religion, I. 56.}}}}
'''2.''' Pertaining to or resembling a shadow or shadows; shadowy.
{{smaller block|<poem>Shadows have their figure, motion,
And their ''umbratile'' action from the real
Posture and motion of the body’s act.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' Unreal; unsubstantial.
{{smaller block|This life that we live disjoyned from God is but a shadow and ''umbratil'' imitation of that.
{{right|''Dr. H. More'', Philos. Poems, p. 337, notes.}}}}

'''umbration''' (um-brā′sho̤n), ''n.'' [< LL. ''umbratio(n-)'', a shading, shadowing, < L. ''umbrare'', pp. ''umbratus'', shade: see ''umbrate''.] '''1.''' A foreshadowing; adumbration.
{{smaller block|Nor all this by transient and superficial knowledge, figures, and ''umbrations'', but immediate and intuitive notices.
{{right|''Evelyn'', True Religion, I. 241.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''her.'', same as ''adumbration''.

'''umbratious†''' (um-brā′shus), ''a.'' [Irreg. var. of ''umbrageous'', after ''umbratic'', etc.: see ''umbrageous''.] Apt to take umbrage; tetchy. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Age, . . . which . . . is commonly . . . ''umbratious'' and apprehensive.{{right|''Sir H. Wotton'', Reliquiæ.}}}}

'''umbra-tree''' (um′brä̤-trē), ''n.'' Same as ''bella-sombra-tree''.

'''umbre''', ''n.'' See ''umber''<sup>1</sup>.

'''umbrel''' (um′brel), ''n.'' [< OF. ''ombrelle'', an umbrella: see ''umbrella''. In def. 3 confused with the form ''umbrere'', which is used in the same sense.] '''1†.''' An umbrella.
{{smaller block|Each of them besides bore their ''umbrels.''
{{right|''Shelton'', tr. of Don Quixote, i. 8. (''Latham.'')}}}}
'''2†.''' A lattice. ''Halliwell.''—'''3.''' A defense for the
face, attached to a helmet. Also called ''shade.'' See also cut under ''armet.''

[[File:century v08 p0378 c2f1.png|center|153px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Helmet with Umbrel, 16th century. (From “L’Art pour Tous.”)}}}}

'''umbrella''' (um-brel′ä̤), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''umbrello'' (also ''umbrel'', q. v.); < It. ''ombrella'', ''umbrella'', an umbrella, sunshade, dim. of ''ombra'', shade, < L. ''umbra'', shade: see ''umbra''. Cf. ''umbracle'', ''umbel'', ''umbella''.] '''1.''' A portable shade, screen, or canopy which opens and folds, carried in the hand for the purpose of sheltering the person from the rays of the sun or from rain. {{smaller|The name was formerly given to a sort of fan used to protect the face from the sun, but is now applied to a light canopy of silk, cotton, or other cloth, extended on a folding frame composed of bars or strips of steel, cane, etc., which slides on a rod or stick. A small and light form of umbrella, carried by women as a protection from the rays of the sun, often in gay colors, or ornamented with ribbons, lace, etc., is habitually called a ''parasol''. The umbrella had its origin in very remote times in the far East, and in some Asiatic countries it was (and still is) regarded as an emblem of royalty or a mark of distinction. In ancient Greece its use was familiar among women for protection from the sun, and it is frequently represented in vase-paintings and terra-cottas. As a defense from rain or snow it was not used in western Europe till early in the eighteenth century. The word is sometimes used figuratively. Compare ''cloak''.}}
{{smaller block|''Umbrellaes'', that is, things that minister shadow unto them [Italians] for shelter against the scorching heate.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 135.}}
''Umbrello'' (Ital. ''Ombrella''), a fashion of round and broad Fans, wherewith the Indians (and from them our great ones) preserve themselves from the heat of the sun or fire; and hence any little shadow, Fan, or other thing wherewith women guard their faces from the sun.
{{right|''Blount'', Glossographia (1670).}}
<poem>The tuck’d up sempstress walks with hasty strides,
While streams run down her oil’d ''umbrella’s'' sides.</poem>
{{right|''Swift'', A City Shower.}} The inseparable gold ''umbrella'', which in that country [Burma] as much denotes the grandee as the star or garter does in England.
{{right|''J. W. Palmer'', Up and Down the Irrawaddi, p. 90.}}}}
{{smaller block|Moreover, he [Jonas Hanway] is said to have been the first man who made a practice [about 1750] of using an ''umbrella'' while walking in the streets of London.
{{right|''Dict. Nat. Biog.'', XXIV. 313.}}}}

'''2.''' In ''zoöl.'': (''a'') The gelatinous disk or swimming-bell of an acaleph, as a jellyfish, by the rhythmical contraction and expansion of which the creature swims, taken either with or without the velum. {{smaller|It is usually the largest, most symmetrical, and most coherent part of the jellyfish, from which other parts hang like streamers, either around its margin or from the center of the under surface. If we compare this bell to a woman’s sun-umbrella, lined as well as covered with silk, and having a fringe, then the outer or aboral surface is the ''exumbrella;'' the inner or under lining surface is the ''adumbrella'', or adoral surface surrounding the mouth, from which large mouth-parts may hang in the position of the stick or handle of the umbrella; the ring of metal which slides up and down the stick may represent the gastric cavity of the creature, and the metal ribs of the umbrella may suggest the radial canals which go out to the circumference. At points around the margin are the series of adradial, perradial, and interradial sense-organs or other appendages, as tentacles, and where these are long and streaming they represent the fringe of the imagined parasol. See cuts under ''acaleph'', ''Aurelia'', ''Discophora'', and ''Willsia''.}}
{{smaller block|In . . . [''Discophora''], the aboral end of the hydranth is dilated into a disk or ''umbrella'', which is susceptible of rhythmical contractile movements.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Invert., p. 118.}}}} (''b'') In ''conch.'' [NL. (Lamarck, 1809).] (1) [''cap.''] A genus of tectibranchiate or pleurobranchiate gastropods; the umbrella-shells, as ''U. umbellata.'' Also ''Ombrella.'' (2) A limpet-like tectibranchiate gastropod of the genus ''Umbrella'' or family ''Umbrellidæ;'' an umbrella-shell.
{{smaller block|The ''umbrellas'' are very large creatures, wearing a flat limpet on the middle of the back, not immersed in the mantle. ''P. P. Carpenter,'' Lect. on
{{right|[Mollusca (1861), p. 86.}}}} {{img float|file=century v08 p0378 c3f1.png|width=61px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Umbrella-shell (''Umbrella umbellata'').}}}}

'''umbrella-ant''' (um-brel′ä̤-ȧnt), ''n.'' A parasol-ant or leaf-carrying ant, which when foraging carries bits of leaves over its back as though for protection, as the sauba-ant, ''Œcodoma cephalotes''. See ''sauba-ant''.
